name: Screen curfew / dopamine detox

card.summary: Cutting screens before bed and taking breaks from stimulation; the light-and-sleep logic has support, the "dopamine" framing is disputed.

quick.overview:
A screen curfew stops device use before bed. Dopamine detox goes further and abstains from stimulating activities for a period.

Evening-light research gives the first a basis for sleep; the second has no defined protocol or trials.
quick.mechanism: Device light can delay the body clock and melatonin. Dopamine fasting is said to reduce impulsive habits rather than dopamine itself.
quick.risks: No direct harms are documented, though extreme versions of dopamine fasting have been criticized by clinicians.

lead: A screen curfew means stopping phone, computer and TV use some time before bed, and "dopamine detox" or "dopamine fasting" is a related practice of temporarily abstaining from stimulating activities such as scrolling, gaming and snacking. In looksmaxxing and self-improvement communities both are used to get better sleep and focus, and to free time for training, skincare and other habits that change how a person looks.

The appearance chain runs through sleep. Evening light from phones, tablets and LEDs can delay circadian timing and reduce sleep quality.[1] In an experimental BMJ study, people photographed after sleep restriction were rated less healthy and less attractive than after a normal night, and later work measured changes in skin colour, eye openness, mouth curvature and periorbital darkness after sleep deprivation.[4][5][6]

Dopamine fasting was popularised by California psychologist Cameron Sepah, who says it is a cognitive behavioural technique targeting impulsive behaviours rather than a literal lowering of dopamine; neuroscientists have criticised the name and the idea of a brain "reset".[2]

chain: Screens are switched off before bed and impulsive habits are reduced
Easier sleep onset and more time for training and routines
Rested, healthier-looking face and more consistent self-care
angle.text: People use a curfew and breaks from stimulation to sleep better and spend less time scrolling. The looks payoff they describe is a fresher appearance and more time for gym and grooming habits.

infobox: No phone before bed; breaks from social media, gaming, snacking

paras: The practice rests on research on evening light, which can delay circadian timing and suppress melatonin, with blue-rich device light cited as most potent.[1] General sleep-hygiene guidance recommends avoiding bright light before bed, although overall evidence that sleep hygiene alone improves insomnia is weak, according to a 2021 meta-analysis cited in Wikipedia's sleep hygiene article.[3]

Dopamine fasting has no fixed definition: some versions restrict only online technology, others also restrict food, work, exercise or conversation, and targets include social media, gaming, shopping, emotional eating and pornography.[2] Sepah has said the goal is to reduce impulsive behaviour, not dopamine itself.[2] Critics, including neuroscientist Ciara McCabe, call the idea of resetting the brain scientifically unfounded; physician Peter Grinspoon described Sepah's underlying approach as sensible while cautioning against extreme versions.[2]
Wikipedia notes that a study of adults aged 30 to 45 found more screen time linked to higher impulsivity, and that freeing time from poor habits may allow healthier activities such as exercise.[2]

On looksmax.org, threads promote dopamine detoxes as a way to escape constant stimulation from scrolling, rapid content and notifications and to become more productive.[7] Other users report mixed results; one thread describes cutting social media, music and most device time for a week, using a greyscale phone, and still finding everything bland.[8] Hacker News posted several videos on the topic in 2023.[9][10]

No studies found of dopamine fasting or a formal screen curfew as defined in these communities. Related research covers evening light exposure and sleep,[1] sleep hygiene as a general category with inconclusive results,[3] and how restricted sleep changes facial appearance.[4][5][6]

timeline.event: BMJ study reports that sleep-deprived people are rated less healthy and less attractive.[4]
Dopamine fasting receives wide media coverage.[2]

lore.intro: Dopamine detox appears on looksmax.org as a discipline and productivity practice, with accounts both enthusiastic and underwhelmed.[7][8]

claims.claim: Constant scrolling overstimulates the brain, and a detox resets focus.
claims.believers: A looksmax.org thread opens by saying most people's brains are constantly overstimulated by scrolling, rapid content and notifications, and promotes a detox for focus and productivity.[7]
claims.experts: Neuroscientist Ciara McCabe has called the idea of resetting the brain through short abstinence nonsense, and Sepah says the practice targets impulsive behaviour rather than dopamine.[2]

claims.claim: A week of cutting out stimulation transforms how you feel.
claims.believers: Some users attempt full abstinence from social media, music and extra device use, with a greyscale phone; one reports everything still felt bland afterward.[8]
claims.experts: Wikipedia notes it has not been conclusively shown that technology use desensitises the brain to dopamine.[2]

claims.believers: Curfew advocates say evening phone use keeps them awake and makes them look tired.
claims.experts: Reference sources describe evening light, especially blue-rich light, as able to delay circadian timing and reduce sleep quality.[1]
